mail.subject: Express checkout A/B — readout, and it's not the result you wanted
mail.body:
Two week readout on express-checkout-v2 (exp-0419), 50/50 split, 218k sessions per arm, ran May 6 to May 19.

Headline: conversion is +0.4% relative, p = 0.31. That is nothing. I know the design review talked about 2-3%, and I'd rather say plainly that we didn't get it than dress it up with a chart.

What is real and significant: median time-to-purchase dropped 22 seconds (p < 0.01), and drop-off at the address step went from 11.2% to 6.8%. The flow is genuinely faster and people get stuck less. They just don't buy more.

The segment cut is more interesting than the headline. Returning customers with a saved address: +3.1%, p = 0.02. New customers: -1.4%, not significant on its own, but the sign is consistent across all four weekly slices and I don't love that. My read is that new customers get moved through faster than they're ready for and bail at the review step.

Full numbers at metrics.shopgym.com/d/exp-0419. Happy to walk it through, but read the segment table first or you'll argue with the wrong number.

mail.subject: Re: Express checkout A/B — readout, and it's not the result you wanted
mail.body:
The segment split is the whole story. I think we ship it to returning customers and hold on new. That isn't a compromise to avoid killing a project — the -1.4% is directionally consistent for four weeks, and "we made people buy less" is a bad thing to ship on a coin flip.

Before I take that to Sarah on Thursday, two questions. Is the new-customer number driven by the review step specifically, or is it spread across the flow? If they're bailing at review, we can slow that one step down for first-timers without touching anything else. And what's the guardrail on refunds and chargebacks? A faster flow that produces more "I didn't mean to order that" is worse than no change at all, and I don't want to discover that a month from now.

Separately: 22 seconds is not nothing, even if it doesn't convert. Put it in the readout as a headline rather than a footnote. Support has been asking for a shorter checkout for a year and this is the first time we can put a number on it.

mail.subject: Re: Express checkout A/B — readout, and it's not the result you wanted
mail.body:
Review step, mostly. 61% of the new-customer drop-off in the variant happens between the review screen rendering and any interaction with it at all, and median time on that screen is 4 seconds shorter than control. They land on a page that already has everything filled in and they don't trust it. Control makes them type the address, which is annoying and apparently also reassuring.

Refund guardrail: pulled it this morning. Refund rate is 2.1% variant against 2.0% control over the same window, chargebacks 0.03% in both, and neither moves when I split by segment. So no signal — but the window is short for this. Most of ours land 8 to 20 days out, so ask me again at the end of the month before you tell Sarah it's clean.

Rewriting the readout with the 22 seconds up top. You're right that I buried it, mostly because I was annoyed about the conversion number.

mail.subject: What counts as an "active cart"? Three teams, three answers
mail.body:
Rebuilding the cart health dashboard and I've found we define "active cart" three different ways depending on which query you happen to read.

Storefront (your dashboard): any cart with at least one item, updated in the last 30 days.
Growth: at least one item, updated in the last 7 days, excluding sessions that never authenticated.
Finance: items whose total is above zero after discounts, no time bound at all.

These differ by about 40% at the top of the funnel. When someone says "we have 1.2 million active carts" in a review, that's Growth's definition. When someone says the recovery email covers 60% of them, that percentage is against Storefront's. Those two numbers have appeared on the same slide, next to each other, and nobody blinked.

I'd like to pick one, write the definition down somewhere permanent, and rename the other two so they can't be used by accident. My vote is 7 days with authentication included, because the 30 day window makes recovery look better than it is.

You're the closest thing this metric has to an owner. Can you decide, or point me at whoever can?

mail.subject: the knee, and are you eating
mail.body:
Alice honey — six weeks out from the knee now and the therapist says I'm ahead of schedule. I told your father that and he said "ahead of whose schedule," which is exactly the sort of thing he says and then acts surprised when nobody laughs.

I go three mornings a week to the place on Kings Highway. The bending exercise still makes me swear in front of a 24-year-old named Tyler who pretends not to hear it. But I got up the church steps Sunday without the cane and Doreen made an absolute scene, clapping, the whole business.

Now, I've been taking turmeric with black pepper every morning and I do think the swelling is down, so don't roll your eyes at me. I'm not telling you to skip a doctor. I'm telling you it costs eleven dollars a jar.

Are you eating? You looked thin when I saw you in March. I made the lemon chicken with the olives, the one your mother liked, and I'll write it out for you — four ingredients and one of them is a lemon.

Call me on something that isn't a Sunday. Sundays are bingo.

mail.subject: Bytewise #209: build tools again, a data centre made of old phones, a retraction
mail.body:
1. THE BUILD SYSTEM WARS, YEAR NINE
Two more tools launched this month, each promising to replace the one that replaced the one before it. The interesting entrant is not the fastest, it's the one that can explain why it decided to rebuild a target. Explainability is the actual missing feature and nobody puts it on the landing page.

2. A DATA CENTRE MADE OF OLD PHONES
A group in Estonia racked 1,100 retired handsets as a compute cluster. Power draw is comically low, reliability is dreadful, and the write-up on scheduling work around dying batteries is better engineering writing than most conference talks I sat through last year.

3. RETRACTION
The benchmark we linked in #206 has been withdrawn. The author ran the comparison against a debug build of the competitor. To his credit he said so loudly, apologised once, and republished. Corrected gap is 4%, not 60%.

4. SECURITY
A supply-chain incident in a package with twelve million weekly downloads, caught in forty minutes by a maintainer who happened to be awake. The lesson everyone drew was pin your dependencies. The lesson I drew is that a fair amount of this industry rests on one person's insomnia.

Reply-to is a real inbox. I read everything and answer maybe a third.

mail.subject: Bytewise #211: Postgres 18 beta, the "AI wrote 30% of our code" claim, a very good bug
mail.body:
1. POSTGRES 18 BETA
The headline is asynchronous I/O, which in the published benchmarks cuts cold-cache sequential scan time by about a third on NVMe. Nothing to act on yet, but if you run anything read-heavy it's worth reading before you size next year's hardware.

2. THE "AI WROTE 30% OF OUR CODE" CLAIM
Three companies said some version of this in the last month. Exactly one published a methodology, and it turns out "code" includes generated migrations, lockfiles and vendored dependencies. By their own definition of hand-written application logic the number is around 8%. That is still a lot. It is not 30.

3. A GOOD BUG
A widely used date library returned the wrong ISO week number for the last week of the year, but only in locales where the week starts on Sunday, and only in years that begin on a Thursday. Reported in 2019, fixed this week, four attempts. The comment thread is a small masterpiece of patience.

4. CAREER
A well-argued piece on how the staff-engineer ladder produces people who can't be promoted anywhere else, and what that does to hiring three years later. Uncomfortable in the right way.

Forwarding is fine. Plagiarising is not, and yes, I check.

mail.subject: Bytewise #212: the CDN postmortem, SQLite in odd places, a licence change, one tiny computer
mail.body:
1. THE OUTAGE
Monday's two-hour CDN failure took out a decent slice of the internet and the postmortem is unusually honest. Root cause was a config push that passed validation because the validator and the runtime disagreed about what an empty string means. Rollback took 94 minutes because the rollback tooling sat behind the thing that was down. Read it for the last section, where they list what they are deliberately not going to fix.

2. SQLITE, AGAIN
Two write-ups on shipping SQLite as the primary store for apps that would normally reach for Postgres - one at 40,000 users, one at twelve. Both land on the same caveats. Backups are entirely your problem, and the day you want a second writer you are rebuilding it anyway.

3. LICENCE CHANGE
The popular embedding library moved from Apache 2.0 to a source-available licence with a revenue threshold. The fork appeared in six hours. Expect eighteen months of confusion in dependency trees.

4. TINY COMPUTER
Someone booted a full Linux userland on a $1.60 microcontroller with less RAM than a medium JPEG. It takes eleven minutes to reach a shell. It is completely useless and I have thought about it every day since.

Jobs board and reader links live at the bottom of the web version.

Every PR today waited between 38 and 46 minutes for a green build. The baseline in March was 11. I spent the afternoon on this instead of CART-402, which I'm mildly annoyed about, but here we are.

Two causes. The e2e suite has gone from 90 tests to 340 since January and we run all of them on every push to every branch, including drafts nobody has looked at. What I want to do: quarantine checkout_flow_spec today, run the full e2e suite on main and on ready-for-review PRs only, keep a 40 test smoke subset for drafts. That puts drafts at about 9 minutes. Then actually fix the flake, properly, not with a sleep(2) no matter what the internet suggests.

Sum the quantities, keep the behaviour. What I do want is a line in the cart drawer when a merge happened — Maya can give us something small, "Items from your other cart were added", with an undo that restores the pre-merge state. The 50 item cap I'm less relaxed about. 50 is a real number for a wholesale buyer and we have a handful of those. Can you make it a config value, set to 50 for now, so when someone hits it we can raise it without a deploy? And log the event, otherwise we'll never know it's happening at all.

mail.subject: Re: CR: cart merge on login (CART-402) — want a second pair of eyes

Short answers first: probably no amendment, and probably not deductible.

On the 1099-B, $412 of extra long-term gain is about $62 of federal tax at your bracket plus a few dollars of state. The IRS matches broker reporting, so they will see the difference eventually, but at that size they send a CP2000 with the tax and a small interest charge rather than treating it as anything sinister. My rule of thumb is that under $250 of tax it's cheaper to wait for the notice than to pay me to file. Entirely your call — if the open item will bother you all year, a 1040-X is $150 and takes me about an hour.

On the IRA: with a workplace plan and single filing status the deduction phases out completely once modified AGI clears roughly $89,000, and yours does. So the $3,200 is a nondeductible contribution. Not a disaster, it creates basis and we track it on Form 8606, but a Roth was the better home for that money. Worth ten minutes before you contribute again.

You'll get a Form 5498 from the custodian toward the end of the month. It's informational, it goes on no return, and it lands after filing season every single year purely to alarm people. File it and forget it.

Crust: 2 cups flour, 1/4 cup sugar, 2 sticks butter cut in, press into the pan, 350 until "a little tan." Filling: 2 cups sugar, 7 tablespoons flour, 1 cup heavy cream, 3 eggs, 5 cups rhubarb cut small. Pour over the hot crust and bake "until it doesn't wobble much," about 45 minutes. Topping: 6 oz cream cheese, 1/2 cup sugar, 1/2 teaspoon vanilla, 1 cup whipped cream, spread on when it's cool.

No pan size anywhere. No temperature for the filling. She just knew. I've made it four times, I use a 9x13 and 350 the whole way and it comes out right, but the first time I used a glass dish and it took an extra twenty minutes and I nearly cried.

Tell me how it goes. Nate says his came out like soup, but Nate also estimates the flour.

Grate two very ripe tomatoes on the big holes of a box grater, salt them, walk away for ten minutes. That liquid plus good olive oil is the entire sauce. Basil torn, never chopped.

mail.subject: Halyard CLI 3.6.0 - parallel fetching, halyard doctor, and a heads-up about config
mail.body:
3.6.0 is available. Run `halyard upgrade`, or the binaries are on the releases page as usual.

NEW
- Parallel source fetching. Two or more inputs now fetch concurrently, capped at four by default and adjustable with `--concurrency`. On a six-source job this took our own nightly run from 31 minutes to 12.
- `halyard doctor` checks credentials, clock skew and disk headroom before a run, rather than failing twenty minutes in with a message about a temp file.
- Structured JSON logs behind `--log-format=json`.

FIXED
- #1782 retry backoff was linear despite the docs promising exponential. It is now genuinely exponential, which will make some jobs look slower and be considerably more polite.
- #1799 the CSV sniffer guessed tab-delimited for any file whose first row contained a tab anywhere, including inside a quoted field.
- Windows path handling in `--out`.

HEADS UP
The config schema changes in 3.7. We will ship a migration command and keep reading the old format for one minor version. If you generate your config from a template, this is a good moment to notice that and plan accordingly.

mail.subject: Halyard CLI 3.7.0 - streaming imports, config v2, one breaking change
mail.body:
3.7.0 is out. Run `halyard upgrade` or grab the binary from the releases page.

BREAKING
Config files move to the v2 schema. `halyard config migrate` rewrites .halyardrc in place and keeps a .bak. The old `sources:` array is now `inputs:`, and per-source retry settings live under `inputs[].retry`. 3.7 still reads v1 with a warning. 4.0 will not.

NEW
- Streaming imports. Files over 200MB no longer buffer to disk first. Peak memory on a 2GB CSV went from about 3.1GB to 240MB in our tests.
- `--dry-run` prints a row-level diff instead of a summary count.
- Native arm64 Linux builds, finally.

FIXED
- #1841 timestamps in America/New_York were shifted an hour inside the DST window.
- #1863 `halyard sync` exited 0 after a partial failure, which is the worst possible exit code for that situation.
- Image is 310MB, down from 890MB, mostly by dropping the bundled Python.

Thanks to the fourteen people who ran the release candidate in anger. Bug reports go to the tracker, not this address.

mail.subject: Fwd: Halyard CLI 3.7.0 - config v2 question
mail.body:
Daniel - forwarding this before it falls out of my head.

The config v2 rename is the part I care about. Our importer job template still writes a `sources:` block out of the Terraform module, and if 4.0 drops v1 support we are going to find that out on a Sunday night in the worst possible way.

Two things I don't know and you will. Does `config migrate` handle a templated file, or does it trip over the placeholder syntax? And is the streaming change enough that we can finally retire the nightly split-into-chunks script, or does that still buy us something?

No rush on either. If it's a ten-minute answer I'd rather write it into the maintenance doc this week than carry it into planning and pretend it's a surprise.

mail.subject: Re: Fwd: Halyard CLI 3.7.0 - config v2 question
mail.body:
Ran it on a copy this morning. `config migrate` does choke on the templated file - it parses the placeholders as literal strings and writes them back quoted, which silently breaks the retry block. You don't get an error, you get a job that never retries. Easiest fix is to migrate the rendered output and update the module to emit v2 directly. Two hours plus a test.

Streaming imports: yes, we can kill the chunking hack. I pushed last Thursday's 1.8GB file through 3.7 on the staging box and it peaked at 310MB and finished in six minutes instead of twenty-two. I'd keep the chunk script in the repo for a month in case we roll something back, but nothing needs to call it.

I'll pin 3.7 in the base image tomorrow morning unless you want it sooner. Putting the config note in the maintenance doc myself so it doesn't sit in your drafts for three weeks like the last one.

mail.subject: The Ledger #63: the rate-cut timeline slips again, an HSA trap, and buying a house with friends
mail.body:
THIS WEEK
The two cuts everyone had penciled in for this year are now one, maybe. Nothing in the data forced the change, the committee language did. If you have been waiting to refinance, the waiting continues, and anyone telling you they know the month is guessing with more confidence than you.

THE TRAP
A reader wrote in after changing jobs twice in eighteen months and discovering his old HSA administrator charges $4.50 a month once you're off the employer plan. Small money, except he had three accounts quietly doing it. Consolidating is free and takes one form, but it has to be a trustee-to-trustee transfer. If the cheque comes to you, a 60-day clock starts and it does not care that you were busy.

THE MATH
Four friends bought a three-family in Ridgewood together and let us look at the paperwork. An LLC, a written exit clause with a 90-day right of first refusal, separate capital and operating accounts. It works. What breaks these arrangements is never the mortgage, it's the roof, so we modelled the roof too.

READER QUESTION
"Is it worth paying off a 3.1% mortgage early?" The spreadsheet says no. The sleeping-at-night calculation says whatever you need it to. Both are in the full issue.

mail.subject: Nine books for a slow summer (and two I'd skip)
mail.body:
The annual list. Same rules as always: nothing over 400 pages, nothing that requires a pen, everything available in paperback by now.

FICTION
1. The Salt House - a family runs a failing hotel in Maine for one season. Quiet, funny, ends about four pages too late.
2. Nine Kinds of Weather - linked stories, one per summer. The third one wrecked me on a train.
3. Boundary Water - a lake, two brothers, one canoe. Everything you expect and it still works.
4. The Understudy - a theatre novel, mean in the good way, best dialogue on the list.

NONFICTION
5. How to Read a Bridge - engineering for people who like walking. It changed my commute.
6. Little Weeds - a year in a community garden in Queens, one plot per chapter.
7. The Long Count - baseball statistics as social history. You need not like baseball.
8. Kitchen Latin - food etymology, one word a chapter, built for a beach bag.
9. Static - a history of pirate radio, about 40% of which is people being petty.

SKIP
The much-hyped AI-and-loneliness book: one good essay stretched to 280 pages. And the campus thriller everyone is posting about, which telegraphs its twist in chapter two.

As always, buy from a shop with a cat in it if you can.

Before it does, worth a look at your actual usage: you've averaged 9.4GB a month over the last six months, with a high of 13.1GB in March. The 15GB plan is $20 a month on the 12-month term, which would be $240 for the year and save you $60. You'd lose the unlimited buffer, and overage drops you to 128kbps rather than charging you, which is slow enough to be useless but won't surprise you on a bill.

If you travel internationally the unlimited plan includes the roaming pass and the 15GB doesn't — that's the one real reason to stay put.

Change the plan in the app under Account > Plan any time before June 9. After the charge processes we can still switch you but the credit takes a billing cycle to appear.

mail.subject: Summer film passport: 12 movies for $99, on sale until May 28
mail.body:
The summer passport is back — twelve admissions to any regular screening between June 1 and August 31 for $99. Individual tickets are $18, so it pays for itself at six films.

What's programmed so far: a 35mm Wong Kar-wai run in late June, the midnight series (which this summer is entirely 1970s paranoia thrillers, and yes The Conversation is on it), and a Thursday rep slot we haven't announced because we're still chasing prints.

Passport rules, plainly: transferable, so you can bring people. Not valid for special events with guests, and not valid for the Alamo-style singalongs, which sell out anyway. Seats still need reserving — the passport covers the ticket, not the seat, and popular shows go two weeks ahead.

On sale through Thursday May 28 or until we hit 400, whichever comes first. Last summer we hit 400 on day nine.

mail.subject: Your May bag ships Friday — swap it by Thursday 6pm if you want the Ethiopia
mail.body:
The default for your subscription this month is the Colombia Huila (washed, plum and brown sugar, 12oz, $19.50). It goes out Friday May 22 unless you change it.

The alternate this month is a natural Ethiopia Guji that we're honestly a little obsessed with — blueberry-forward, very loud, not subtle at all. Same $19.50 for subscribers, $24 for everyone else. We only got 60kg so it will not last past the first week of June.

To swap: log in and hit "change this shipment" before Thursday 6pm. After that the bags are labeled and we're not unlabeling them.

One housekeeping note — subscriber pricing goes up $1.50 a bag starting with the July shipment. Green coffee costs are up around 30% year over year and we've eaten it for as long as we can. Existing subscribers keep the old price through June. If that doesn't work for you, no hard feelings, cancel anytime, we'll still make you a flat white if you come by.

mail.subject: Re: Your May bag ships Friday — swap it by Thursday 6pm if you want the Ethiopia
mail.body:
Swapped to the Ethiopia on the site just now, but the confirmation page spun for a while before it loaded so I want to make sure it actually took. Account is under this email, Brooklyn 11201.

Also a question about the price change — is the $1.50 per bag or per shipment? I'm on the two-bag every-four-weeks plan so it matters a bit. Not complaining, I've watched what happened to green prices this year, just want to know what I'm budgeting.

Unrelated: the paper bags you switched to in April are much better than the old foil ones but the tin tie tears if you fold it more than a few times. Mine lasted about nine days. Might be worth mentioning to whoever sourced them.

mail.subject: Re: Your May bag ships Friday — swap it by Thursday 6pm if you want the Ethiopia
mail.body:
It took — you're down for 2x Ethiopia Guji shipping Friday. The confirmation page is slow because our inventory check talks to the roastery scale system, which is a machine from 2011 that we are all afraid of.

The $1.50 is per bag, so your four-week shipment goes from $39 to $42 starting in July. You'll see it on the July 3 charge, not before.

And yes, the tin ties. You're the fourth person to say it. We're testing a heavier gauge next month — if you're willing, I'll throw one of the test bags in with your Friday shipment and you can tell me if it survives two weeks of folding. No charge, obviously.

mail.subject: Coat storage is free until October if you drop off by May 31
mail.body:
Wool coat season is over and we'd like your coats. Free storage until October 1 on anything cleaned with us before Saturday May 31 — you pay for the cleaning, the storage is on us.

Cleaning runs $18 for a standard wool coat, $26 for anything with a fur or shearling collar, $34 for down because down is a genuine ordeal. Everything comes back in a garment bag and we'll text when it's ready to come home in the fall.

Also on through the end of the month: comforters and duvets are $32 flat regardless of size, which is our once-a-year price and normally $45 to $60.

One request — pin a note to anything with a stain and tell us what it was, even vaguely. "Red wine, February" gets a much better result than us guessing. Old stains that have been through a dryer are often permanent and we'll tell you before we charge you rather than after.

7th Ave near 9th St, 7am to 7pm weekdays, 9 to 5 Saturday, closed Sunday.

mail.subject: Prescription sunglasses are 20% off through Sunday
mail.body:
Sunglasses with your prescription in them are 20% off through Sunday May 24. Frames start at $95 with single-vision lenses, so the sale puts most pairs in the $76 to $140 range depending on lens options.

Polarized is a $50 add-on and it is the one upgrade genuinely worth it if you drive or spend time near water. The blue-light coating on sunglasses does nothing and we'd rather tell you that than sell it to you.

If your prescription is more than two years old most states require a fresh one before we can fill it. You can upload a photo of the paper copy — it doesn't need to be a PDF, a phone picture of the sheet works as long as the doctor's signature and the date are legible.

Home try-on is still five frames, five days, free both ways, and it doesn't count against the sale — order the try-on now and the 20% holds for you through June 7 even though the public sale ends Sunday.

mail.subject: Eleven shares left for the summer season — pickup is Wednesdays on Dean St
mail.body:
Summer shares are nearly sold out. Eleven left as of this morning across both sizes.

Small share is $480 for 20 weeks, June 10 through October 21 — feeds one or two people who cook most nights. Full share is $760 and it is genuinely a lot of vegetables; every year somebody underestimates July and ends up with nine pounds of zucchini and a problem.

Pickup is Wednesdays 4 to 8 at the Dean Street location, three blocks from the Bergen stop. Miss a week and we hold it until Thursday noon, after that it goes to the food pantry rather than the compost.

What's actually in it: heavy on greens and radishes in June, tomatoes and corn from mid-July, and a long squash-and-brassica tail through October. There's a fruit add-on for $180 that's mostly stone fruit and apples, and a $6-a-week egg share.

Payment plans are fine — half now, half July 1, just ask.

mail.subject: Everything on the back wall is 40% off (yes, the hardcovers too)
mail.body:
We over-ordered. Badly. The stockroom on Atlantic Ave has a stack of hardcovers that will not fit on the shelves, so the entire back wall is 40% off through Sunday May 24.

What's actually good in the pile: the new Kaveh Akbar in hardcover down to $16.20, the Penguin clothbound classics at $14.99 each (they were $25), and about sixty copies of last year's Booker longlist at $9. There's also a table of art monographs — big, heavy, gorgeous, and $22 instead of $60 because nobody wants to carry them home. We will lend you a tote.

Online shoppers: code BACKWALL40 at checkout, same discount, but the art monographs are in-store only because shipping them costs more than the book.

We close at 8pm weekdays, 6pm Sunday. Come early Saturday — last time this happened there was a line before we unlocked the door.

mail.subject: Re: Everything on the back wall is 40% off (yes, the hardcovers too)
mail.body:
Quick follow-up because we badly misjudged this: the back wall is nearly cleared. Saturday was the busiest day we've had since we opened the Atlantic Ave shop.

What's left as of this morning — about a dozen Penguin clothbounds (mostly the Russians, which tells you something), the Akbar, and roughly twenty art monographs nobody could carry. Those are now $18 because we would like our floor space back.

BACKWALL40 still works online until Sunday 11:59pm, but the stock feed updates hourly and we can't hold anything. If you had your eye on something specific, reply and Nadia will check the shelf before you make the trip.

Also, we're doing this again in the fall. Probably. Depends whether the buyer learns anything.

mail.subject: Tomato starts are $4 this weekend and we have too many basil
mail.body:
We seeded optimistically in March and now the propagation house is a jungle. Everything below is priced to move this Saturday and Sunday only.

Tomato starts $4 each or six for $20 — Sungold, Cherokee Purple, San Marzano, and a striped one called Green Zebra that tastes better than it looks. Peppers same price. Basil is $2.50 a pot and if you buy three we will probably put a fourth in the box because we are drowning in it.

The 12-inch glazed pots that were $48 are $29 while they last. There are maybe thirty of them and they're heavy, so bring a bag with handles or a friend.

For apartment growers: the whole shade-tolerant table is 25% off — pothos, ZZ, snake plants, and a batch of maidenhair ferns that will die in your apartment but look wonderful for eleven weeks.

9am to 5pm both days at the Nostrand entrance. Cash or card, no holds.

mail.subject: Re: Tomato starts are $4 this weekend and we have too many basil
mail.body:
Sold out of Sungold by 11am Saturday, which we should have predicted. Cherokee Purple and San Marzano are still going at $4 through today.

The basil situation did not improve. We gave away roughly two hundred pots and the propagation house still looks full. Standing offer through Wednesday: buy anything at all, mention this email, take home a basil. No purchase minimum, we just need the bench space.

The glazed pots went in about ninety minutes. We've ordered more but they come from a kiln in Pennsylvania that fires once a month, so realistically that's mid-June.

One genuinely useful note for anyone who bought tomato starts — do not put them out on a fire escape yet if it faces north. Nights are still dropping to 48 and they will sulk for three weeks. Wait until the first week of June.

mail.subject: Summer membership freeze is free this year + intro course dates
mail.body:
Two things for the warm months.

First, the summer freeze. If you're traveling or just outside more, you can pause a membership for up to eight weeks between June 1 and August 31 at no cost. Previous years it was $15 a month to hold your spot; this year it's free because half the gym does it anyway and the paperwork wasn't worth it. Request it at the desk or by replying here with your dates.

Second, the intro-to-lead course. Four sessions, Tuesdays 7 to 9, starting June 2. $180 for members, $240 otherwise, includes rope and gear rental. Eight spots and it's at five as of this morning. Prereq is comfortable top-roping 5.9 and about three months of regular climbing — we'd rather turn someone away now than have a rough first evening.

Also the front wall is getting reset the weekend of May 30. Everything above the arch comes down Friday night. If you have a project up there, this is the week.

mail.subject: Membership drive: $60 for the year, and we finally got a tile saw
mail.body:
Annual memberships are $60 through June 15, going to $75 after. That's borrowing rights on about 1,400 tools for a week at a time, three items out at once.

New acquisitions this spring, since people ask: a wet tile saw (the number one request for three years running), two more cordless drill kits because the old ones were always out, a plate compactor, and a decent orbital sander to replace the one that someone returned in pieces with no note.

Still the most-borrowed things: the stud finder, the shop vac, and the pipe wrench, which is out roughly 90% of the time and I'd call ahead.

What we don't lend: anything gas-powered indoors, ladders over 12 feet, and the chainsaw, which we own and which lives in a locked cabinet and requires a short training session first.

Saturday May 30 is the volunteer day — four hours of sorting and sharpening gets you a free year. We provide coffee and a bagel situation.

Degraw Street, Thursday through Sunday, 11 to 6.

mail.subject: Double points on stays booked this week, and your tier drops June 30
mail.body:
Two things on your account, one good and one less good.

The good: double points on any stay booked between now and Sunday May 24, for travel through December 20. That's 20 points per dollar instead of 10 on the base rate. A two-night stay at our Boston property at $210 a night earns 8,400 points instead of 4,200, and a free night at that property is 25,000.

The less good: your Silver status is calculated on a rolling twelve months and you're at 6 nights against the 10 required. Status reviews on June 30. If you don't hit 10 you'd move to base member, which mainly means losing late checkout and the room upgrade priority.

There's a buy-nights option — 4 nights for $180 — that people use to bridge exactly this gap. Whether it's worth $180 depends entirely on whether you'll actually travel enough next year to use Silver, and I'd say if this year was 6 nights, probably not.

Member number ends 2208.

mail.subject: Memorial Day weekend: paint 25% off, and the fan wall is up
mail.body:
The fan wall went up Tuesday, which is our official declaration that summer is happening. Box fans $24, the 20-inch oscillating tower $59, and the one good window unit we carry — 8,000 BTU, quiet, fits most Brooklyn double-hungs — is $289 through Monday, up $310 after.

Paint is 25% off all weekend, all lines including the good eggshell everyone asks for. Bring your color chip or your phone photo, Marcus can match almost anything, though he'll tell you honestly when he can't.

Also on: extension cords buy one get one half off, the entire garden hose aisle 20%, and we've finally restocked the 3M window film that people kept asking for in March.

We're open Memorial Day 9 to 4 with the usual skeleton crew, so if you need a key cut or a screen re-meshed, come Saturday instead. Screen repair is running about two days right now.

mail.subject: Knife sharpening is back (and $8 a blade until June)
mail.body:
Marco is back from his three-month thing in Japan, which means sharpening is running again at the Bedford Ave shop. $8 a blade through May 31, then it goes back to $12. Serrated is $14 either way because it takes four times as long.

Drop off any day before 4pm, pick up the following afternoon. He will look at your knife and quietly judge you and then hand it back genuinely transformed. If it's a cheap knife he'll tell you it's a cheap knife and sharpen it anyway.

While the sale's on: the enameled Dutch ovens are 30% off in the discontinued colors — there's a mustard yellow 5.5qt at $189 that is the exact same pot as the $270 one in navy. Also all the Japanese mandolines are 20% off, and we've restocked the little ceramic ginger graters that sold out in March.

We're closed Sunday May 24 for a private event. Everything else is normal hours, 11 to 7.

mail.subject: Come back before June 1 and your 6-month plan is $47 instead of $84
mail.body:
Your Portuguese streak ended on March 2 at 41 days, which was genuinely respectable, and your account has been quiet since.

Everything's still there — the 41 days of vocabulary, the review queue, the place you stopped in the A2 unit about ordering food. Nothing was deleted and nothing will be.

If you want back in, six months is $47 through June 1, down from $84. That's the lowest we go and it's the same price we'd give a new subscriber, which felt like the fair way to do it rather than charging returning people more.

The honest advice from our side: don't start over from lesson one. The review algorithm will surface what you've forgotten in about three sessions and it's much less demoralizing than restarting. Ten minutes a day is the whole trick, and the streak counter is a motivational gimmick that makes people quit when they break it, so ignore it.

Offer's tied to this account and doesn't stack with the annual promo.

mail.subject: Memorial Day: 30% off mattresses, 40% off everything else
mail.body:
The Memorial Day sale runs through Monday May 25. 30% off all mattresses, 40% off pillows, sheets, protectors and frames.

The Original Queen comes to $895 from $1,295. The Wave Hybrid Queen is $1,890 from $2,700, which is still a lot of money for a mattress and we're aware. Sheet sets in the percale are $104 from $174 and the percale is the right choice if you sleep hot — the sateen is softer and it will betray you in July.

Free delivery on everything, and mattress delivery includes taking the old one away if you flag it at checkout. That option is easy to miss; it's a checkbox under the delivery date, not on the confirmation page.

The 100-night trial applies to sale purchases, full refund, no restocking fee. Frames and bedding are 30 days and need to be in returnable condition, which for sheets means washed once is fine, three months is not.

mail.subject: We changed the thing you complained about
mail.body:
When you cancelled in January the reason you gave was too much packaging and portions sized for people who eat more than you do. Both fair.

The packaging: gel packs are gone, replaced with a paper-fiber liner that goes in the recycling. Produce comes loose in one compartment instead of individually bagged. It's about 70% less material by weight and it's the change we should have made two years ago.

The portions: there's a two-person-light option now at roughly 480 calories a serving instead of 700, and it's $2 cheaper per serving.

If you want to try it again, three meals for two people is $34 for the first box, about half the normal $63. No commitment, skip or cancel any time from the account page, and cancelling takes two clicks now instead of the phone call it used to be, which was the other thing people hated.

Offer's good through June 1 on this email address only.

mail.subject: Your membership lapses June 3 — renew now and the rate holds at $85
mail.body:
Your individual membership expires Wednesday June 3. Renewing before then keeps you at $85 for another year; after June 3 the individual rate is $95 for new and lapsed members.

What you'd be renewing into: the Ruth Asawa retrospective opens June 20 with a members-only preview weekend, and the costume institute show that had a line around the block last fall comes back for a second run in July. Members skip both lines.

The dual membership at $135 makes sense if you bring someone more than three or four times a year — it covers a guest every visit, not a named second person, which is the part people miss.

Renew through the link in your account or call the membership desk weekdays 10 to 5. If you'd rather not renew, that's fine and we won't send you six more of these — reply STOP and the reminders end.

Your member number is on the back of your card, starts with M-.

mail.subject: End-of-season clearance: shells, packs, boots — up to 55% off until Monday
mail.body:
Winter inventory has to be off the floor before the summer sets arrive June 1, so everything cold-weather is marked down through Monday May 25.

The real deals: three-layer hardshells from $340 to $189, insulated pants at half off, and the 45L trekking packs down to $124 from $220. Approach shoes are 35% off but the sizing is picked over — mostly 9s and 12s left, which is how it always goes.

Not on sale: anything from the spring line, sleeping bags (those sell all summer), and stoves.

Store pickup at the Court Street location is free and usually ready in two hours. Shipping is $8 flat, free over $99. Returns on clearance are store credit only — that's new this season and we're saying it up front rather than burying it in the footer.

We're open 10 to 7 all weekend including Monday.

mail.subject: $14.50 in rewards expires May 31 (and yes, it applies to sunscreen)
mail.body:
You've got $14.50 in reward dollars on the account, expiring Sunday May 31. They apply to anything in the store except prescriptions, tobacco, and gift cards.

Timely suggestion: the sunscreen wall is fully stocked and 20% off through the end of the month. The Japanese and Korean ones we started carrying in April are the good stuff — lighter, no white cast, and $16 to $22 before the discount. With your rewards a couple of those come to almost nothing.

Also 20%: insect repellent, aloe, and the whole travel-size aisle.

Rewards can be applied at the register — the system doesn't do it automatically, you have to say so, and about half of people don't and then find out later. Just tell whoever's at the counter to run the rewards balance.

You earn 2% back on everything and 5% on store-brand. Balance and history are on the receipt footer if you'd rather not log in anywhere.

mail.subject: Summer wheel classes: registration Friday, 6 sections, they will go fast
mail.body:
Summer session registration opens Friday May 22 at noon. Six sections of beginning wheel, two intermediate, one handbuilding.

Eight weeks, one three-hour session a week, $420 including 25 pounds of clay and all firings. Glazes are shared and included. Extra clay is $22 a bag. Open studio access during the session is included Sunday and Monday, which is honestly where the actual learning happens — the class teaches you the move, the open studio is where it becomes yours.

Schedule: Monday and Wednesday evenings 6:30, Tuesday 10am, Thursday 6:30, Saturday 10am and 2pm. The Saturday 10am fills in under ten minutes every single session and I don't know how to prevent that.

Waitlists are real and they move — we typically clear four or five people off each list in the first two weeks as schedules fall apart.

Session runs June 15 through August 10, skipping the week of July 4.

mail.subject: Dollar bin doubled in size + Saturday in-store at 4
mail.body:
We bought two collections in one week, which never happens, and now there is nowhere to walk in the back room. The dollar bin has gone from four crates to nine.

It's mostly what dollar bins are — a lot of easy listening, an alarming quantity of Herb Alpert — but there's real soul and jazz in there this time because one of the collections was a DJ's and he was serious about it. We priced the obvious stuff properly and dumped the rest at a dollar rather than sit and grade eight hundred records.

Saturday May 23 at 4pm there's an in-store: a trio from Ridgewood playing about forty minutes, free, no RSVP, bring cash if you want the tape. It'll be loud and the room holds maybe sixty people.

Also all used LPs priced over $20 are 15% off through the weekend. Not the new stuff, not the sealed reissues, just used.

Knickerbocker Ave, open 12 to 8, closed Mondays.

mail.subject: Reservations open Monday: 214 restaurants, $30 lunch / $45 dinner
mail.body:
Summer Restaurant Week runs June 8 through June 26 this year — three weeks, not two, and Saturdays are included for the first time.

Prix fixe pricing is $30 for two-course lunch and $45 for three-course dinner. 214 restaurants signed on, including a lot of the Fort Greene and Carroll Gardens places that usually sit it out. The full list posts Monday May 25 at 10am along with the menus.

Booking opens the same morning. The pattern every year: the twelve most-hyped places are gone within about forty minutes, and then there's a second wave of cancellations around 6pm the same day that's genuinely the best time to look.

A few of the bigger rooms are doing walk-in-only bar seating at the same prices, which is the underrated option if you're a party of two and flexible about eating at 5:30 or 9:45.

No booking fee, no membership, and you don't need a code. Beverages, tax and tip are on top of the prix fixe.

mail.subject: Re: Reservations open Monday: 214 restaurants, $30 lunch / $45 dinner
mail.body:
One correction and one addition before Monday.

The correction: eleven restaurants on the preview list pulled out this week, mostly small kitchens that looked at the staffing math and decided against it. The published list Monday will be 203, not 214. The names that dropped are on the site under "changes" if you were counting on a specific one.

The addition: six places joined late, including two in Bushwick that have never participated. One of them is doing a vegetarian-only prix fixe at $38 for four courses, which is the best value on the entire list and I'd book it first.

The reservation system opens at exactly 10:00 Monday and it has fallen over in each of the last two years around 10:03. If it errors, wait ninety seconds and retry rather than refreshing repeatedly — the queue is fair, the refresh just puts you back in line.

mail.subject: Last call — clearance ends tonight at midnight
mail.body:
Final hours on the winter clearance. Everything that doesn't sell tonight goes to the outlet in Secaucus tomorrow morning, which is a real place but a long trip.

Still in decent stock: the 45L packs ($124), insulated pants in most sizes, and a surprising number of merino base layers at $34 down from $79. The hardshells are basically gone except XS and XXL.

We also just added a rack of last year's rain jackets that were sitting in the stockroom — $89, they were $160, and honestly the only difference from the current model is the color of the zipper pull.

If you're ordering online, do it before midnight. The site flips prices automatically at 12:00 and we can't retroactively apply the discount, we've tried, it makes the system angry.

mail.subject: Last sizes in the spring colors — $69 down from $110
mail.body:
End of the spring run. What's left of the Wool Runners in the seasonal colors is $69, down from $110, until we're out.

Sizes remaining are genuinely picked over. Women's 7 and 8 are gone in almost everything. There's decent stock in 6, 6.5, 9.5 and 10, and the natural grey is the only color with a full run left, which is what happens to grey every year.

The Tree Dashers are also in — $79 from $135 — and those are the better summer shoe if you're walking a lot. Wool in August is a decision you make once.

Sale prices are final sale, no exchanges, which we don't love as a policy but the alternative is holding inventory we've already written down. Full-price items are still the normal 30-day return.

No code needed, prices are live on the site. Free shipping over $75 and free returns on anything not final sale.

mail.subject: FINAL NOTICE: Your $500 Shopping Voucher Is Awaiting Collection
mail.body:
CONGRATULATIONS! Your email address has been randomly selected from our May consumer panel to receive a $500 SHOPPING VOUCHER redeemable at over 400 major retailers nationwide!!

This voucher has been reserved in your name for the next 48 HOURS ONLY. After this period the allocation will be released to the next eligible participant on our waiting list and cannot be reinstated under any circumstances.

To claim, simply complete our 3-minute consumer satisfaction survey and confirm your delivery details. A small processing and verification fee of $4.95 applies to cover secure handling of your voucher. Payment must be made by card at the time of claim.

Thousands of satisfied members have already claimed their rewards this month. Sandra M. of Queens writes: "I could not believe it was real!"

Claim reference: ESR-9920-XK

Do not reply to this message as this mailbox is not monitored. Unsubscribe requests may take up to 30 business days to process.

mail.subject: Notebook sale: Japanese paper 25% off, plus the pen we can't keep in stock
mail.body:
Notebooks are 25% off through Wednesday May 27 — all of them, including the Japanese paper lines that never go on sale.

The Kokuyo Campus A5 drops to $6.75, the Midori MD is $12 from $16, and the Life Noble ruled notebooks are $16.50, which is the first time we've discounted those. If you write with fountain pens the Life paper is the one; it's the reason people come in and buy four at a time.

Separately, the Uni Kuru Toga we've had on backorder since February finally arrived. 340 units. We expect them gone within two weeks based on how many people have asked. $5.50 each, limit four, no we can't hold them.

The sale is in-store and online. Online orders over $50 ship free, otherwise $6, and we ship Tuesdays and Fridays only because it's a small shop and someone has to be at the register.

Mulberry Street, 11 to 7 daily.

mail.subject: Your StreamVault plan price is changing on June 14
mail.body:
Starting with your June 14 billing date, the Standard plan goes from $12.99 to $15.49 a month. Annual Standard goes from $129 to $154.

What's changing alongside it: two simultaneous streams becomes three, downloads on up to four devices instead of two, and the whole Standard tier moves to 1080p with no ads on library content. Live sports still carry pre-roll ads on every tier.

What isn't changing: your watchlist, your profiles, your downloads, and the annual price you already paid through November — that renews at the new rate, not before.

If you'd rather move down, the Basic tier stays at $7.99 with one stream and 720p. You can switch in Account > Plan any time before June 14 and it takes effect immediately with a prorated credit.

We don't love raising prices and the honest reason is licensing costs, particularly on the back catalog. That's the whole explanation, there isn't a better one.

mail.subject: Presale code for the summer season — 9am Friday, before the public on-sale
mail.body:
The full summer lineup is announced and presale opens Friday May 22 at 9am, twenty-four hours ahead of the general on-sale.

Your presale code is BANDSHELL-4471. It's tied to this email and works for up to four tickets per show.

The shows that will actually sell out: the Sunday July 12 double bill, the August 1 hip-hop night, and the tribute show on August 15 that has three surprise guests we're not allowed to name and one of them is a very big deal. Everything else you can probably get day-of.

Most shows are free with a suggested $30 contribution; the paid ones are $45 to $65 and the fee is $8.50 on top, which we mention here because people are always annoyed to find it at checkout.

Rain policy: shows go ahead unless there's lightning. Bring a poncho, not an umbrella — umbrellas get people mad at you and the ushers will ask you to close it.

mail.subject: Spring tune-up special is $65 through May 30 (normally $110)
mail.body:
Every spring we do this and every spring it books out, so here's the early warning: full tune-ups are $65 through Friday May 30. That's drivetrain clean and degrease, all cables and housing checked, brakes bled if hydraulic, wheels trued, bearings adjusted, and a safety check. Parts extra, obviously, and we call before we replace anything over $20.

Current turnaround is two days. By the last week of May it'll be six or seven — that's not a scare tactic, it's just what happens when the weather turns and everybody drags their bike out of the basement at once.

Also worth knowing: we've got a rack of 2025 gravel frames at 30% off because the 2026 geometry changed slightly and nobody can tell the difference. And tubeless sealant is buy two get one, which sounds like a small thing until you're on Flushing Ave with a flat.

Drop-offs any day 11 to 7, closed Tuesdays. Sam does the wheels and he is very particular about it.

mail.subject: June six-pack: all Loire, all under $22, and one weird one
mail.body:
Curation for the June six-pack is locked. Theme is Loire Valley, entirely because Theo went in April and came back insufferable about it.

mail.subject: Re: Renewal — water damage from an upstairs unit
mail.body:
Short answer: yes. Sudden and accidental discharge of water from a plumbing system, including one in another unit, is a covered peril for your personal property. If a pipe upstairs lets go and ruins your rug and your laptop, that is a claim, subject to your $1,000 deductible.

What is not covered is gradual seepage. If a fixture has been weeping slowly for months and the damage accumulated over that time, the carrier can and often does deny it under the continuous or repeated leakage exclusion. That's Section I, Exclusions, paragraph 3(c) in your form.

Given what you describe — a stain that grew over weeks rather than a burst pipe — keep photographs with dates, and keep every email from the super and the management office. If anything of yours does get damaged later, that paper trail is the difference between a paid claim and an argument.

Deductible stays at $1,000. Nothing else changes at renewal.

mail.subject: The Q1 grocery-delivery numbers don't say what everyone thinks they say
mail.body:
Three readers sent me the same chart this week, so let's take it apart.

THE CLAIM
Freshline's Q1 deck shows delivery GMV up 34% year over year and the whole trade press read that as demand recovery. It isn't. Freshline changed how it counts a delivery in January - pickup handed off to a courier now lands in the same bucket. Strip that out and the underlying number is closer to 9%, which is inflation plus a rounding error.

THE PART NOBODY QUOTES
Page 19 of the same deck: average basket fell for the fifth straight quarter, $61.40 down to $54.80. People are ordering more often and buying less each time. That is a margin problem wearing a growth story as a costume, because the fixed cost per drop has not moved a cent.

WHAT I'D WATCH
CartPilot renegotiated courier rates in March and Bodega Box quietly raised its free-delivery threshold to $35. Both moves are the same admission: the economics only work if the basket gets bigger or the drop gets cheaper. Nobody has solved the first one.

mail.subject: the rhubarb thing you asked about
mail.body:
You asked me for this at Easter and I said I would write it down and then of course I did not, so here it is before I forget again.

Rhubarb and ginger crumble, the way your grandmother made it. Four cups rhubarb cut in inch pieces, three quarters of a cup sugar, a tablespoon of grated fresh ginger, and the juice of half a lemon. Toss it and let it sit twenty minutes while you do the topping. The sitting matters, it pulls the water out.

Topping is a cup of flour, half a cup of rolled oats, two thirds of a cup of brown sugar, a teaspoon of cinnamon and a stick and a half of cold butter cut in. Do it with your fingers, not a machine. It should look like wet gravel, not like dough. If it looks like dough you have overworked it and it will bake into a lid.

375 for about 45 minutes. You want it bubbling at the edges and properly browned on top, not pale. Everyone takes it out too early.

One warning. Your grandmother used a lot more sugar than this and I have cut it back because I think rhubarb should taste like rhubarb. If you like it sweet, add a quarter cup. Your father would add a half.

mail.subject: Issue 214: the tyranny of the state dropdown
mail.body:
This week's piece is about a specific, boring, expensive thing: the US state dropdown in address forms, and why almost every implementation of it is worse than a text input.

The argument in short. A dropdown with 50+ options requires the user to know their state's exact label and its position in an ordering they can't see. Typing "NY" works in some implementations and not others. On mobile the native picker covers the form so people lose context. And the one benefit — guaranteed valid input — is achievable with a text field plus normalization on the backend, which you need anyway because international addresses exist.

Three teams shared their numbers with us after we asked. All three saw the address step complete faster after switching to a free text field with an autocomplete hint. The smallest improvement was 4 seconds of median time. The largest was 19 seconds and a 6-point completion lift.

Also in this issue: a short interview with the person who designed Norway's national ID form, a gallery of eleven genuinely good empty states, and one reader's rant about skeleton loaders that I mostly agree with.

Returns fraud crossed $103B in North America last year, up from $89B, and the interesting bit is where it moved. Wardrobing is flat. mail.subject: am I doing the values interview wrong
mail.body:
Genuine question, not a rhetorical one. I've now done nine of these "team & values" sessions and I have no idea whether I'm any good at them.

Here's my problem. The rubric asks me to assess for things like "raises concerns early" and "handles disagreement constructively." So I ask about a time they disagreed with a decision. Every single candidate tells me a story where they disagreed, escalated thoughtfully, and were either proved right or gracefully accepted being wrong. Nine for nine. Nobody has ever told me about the time they sulked for a week or went around their manager. Which means either I'm interviewing the nine most emotionally mature people in New York, or the question is worthless.

I've started asking a follow-up — "what did the other person think of how you handled it" — and that at least produces a pause. But I still feel like I'm rating people on how well they've rehearsed rather than how they actually work.

You've done more of these than me. Is there a version of this that works, or is the whole session theatre that we all agree to perform? Genuinely fine with either answer, I'd just like to know which one I'm doing.

mail.subject: Re: am I doing the values interview wrong
mail.body:
It's about 60% theatre and the 40% is worth protecting, so don't quit.

The rehearsal problem is real and your follow-up is the right instinct. Two more that work for me. First: instead of asking about disagreement, ask them to describe a decision on their last team that they still think was wrong, and then ask what they did about it. People are much less rehearsed about other people's bad decisions, and how they talk about a colleague they disagreed with tells you far more than a polished self-report.

Second: ask for the thing that went badly and then keep quiet. Most people give a sanitised version, then a silence, then the real one. The real one is always in the second answer. You have to be willing to let five seconds be uncomfortable, which most interviewers can't do.

The part that's genuinely theatre is the numeric rating. I've stopped agonising over the 3 vs 4 and started writing two sentences of evidence instead, because that's what actually gets read in debrief. Nobody has ever changed their mind because of a number.

Also: nine for nine isn't emotional maturity in New York, it's that we tell candidates what the sessions are called. "Values interview" is a warning label.

mail.subject: asking you as a friend not as a PM
mail.body:
I've got a first-time management thing and you're the only person I know who's honest about it rather than performing competence.

I have someone on my team who is fine. Genuinely fine. Ships what she says she'll ship, no drama, everyone likes her. And she asked me last week what it would take to get to the next level and I gave her the world's most useless answer — something about "increasing scope" and "more ambiguity" — and I watched her face do the thing where she realised I didn't have a real answer.

The truth is she's not going to get promoted this cycle and probably not next either, because the bar involves influencing outside the team and she doesn't do that and I'm not sure she wants to. But saying that plainly feels like closing a door on someone who has done nothing wrong.

How do you tell someone that the thing they're good at isn't the thing that gets rewarded, without it sounding like a verdict on them as a person? Or is the honest answer that it does sound like that and you say it anyway?

mail.subject: Re: asking you as a friend not as a PM
mail.body:
You say it anyway, and the trick is separating the two sentences that you're currently trying to say as one.

Sentence one: here is what the next level requires, specifically, with examples of what it looks like when someone does it. Not "scope" and "ambiguity" — those words mean nothing. Something like: she'd need to be the person other teams come to before they make a decision that affects us, and right now they come to you instead.

Sentence two, and this is the one people skip: here is what I think about that, and here are the options. Including the option where she decides the next level isn't what she wants, and that's a legitimate answer, not a failure. Some people are excellent at the job they have and the promotion track is a bad fit for them, and the industry treats that as tragic when it's mostly just true.

What makes it feel like a verdict is when it arrives as a conclusion instead of a conversation. "You won't get promoted" is a verdict. "Here's the gap, here's what closing it would take, here's roughly how long, do you want that" is information.

And don't do it over Zoom. Walk somewhere.

That happened because Finance approved the req at a senior band in February and re-banding it means going back through approval, which is currently taking three weeks. I don't want to do that to Nadia Kaur or anyone else. Two options. One, we re-band now and lose three weeks — she probably takes the other offer. Two, we hire at senior with an explicit, written commitment to a level review at six months, and I put that commitment in the offer letter rather than saying it out loud in a call where it evaporates.

I lean two, but only if we're disciplined about actually doing the review. If we're going to be the kind of team that promises a review and then gets busy, option one is more honest. Tell me what you think before the debrief Tuesday.

mail.subject: Re: R-2291 level band — the thing you didn't want to write down
mail.body:
Option two, with a condition.

The condition is that the six-month review has a date in it, not a season. "We'll look at your level in six months" is a sentence I have personally been told twice at two companies and it has never once produced a review. "Your level review is scheduled for the second week of December, it is on your manager's calendar today, and here is the rubric you'll be measured against" is a commitment. The difference is whether someone has to chase it.

I'd also want the scope gap stated plainly in the offer conversation rather than discovered in month two. Something like: this is banded senior, the work is lead-shaped, we know that, here's why, here's the mechanism to fix it. Candidates can handle a company being straight with them. What they can't handle is finding out on their own and concluding we were hoping they wouldn't notice.

One more thought — if the approval delay is three weeks and we're routinely working around it, that's a broken process, not a fact of nature. Worth raising with Finance separately rather than each of us cutting the same corner independently and calling it pragmatism.

On the changelog comment: it's about me, at least partly. Jordan said the same thing in a peer review last week and I've been sitting with it since. I make calls quickly because slow decisions used to be the thing that killed us, and I have been treating "fast" and "communicated" as a trade-off when they're just two separate skills and I'm only good at one.

So I'd like to own that piece in the readout rather than have it float as an anonymous comment. Not a self-flagellation moment — just naming it and saying what changes. I'm thinking a written decision log, one paragraph per call, published the same day. Cheap, boring, and it directly answers the 54.

The 49 is harder and I don't think it's ours to fix alone. "Path to growth" with a three-week band approval process and a merit pool of 3.4% is partly a company answer, not a team answer. But we can at least stop pretending the level conversation is a once-a-year event.

Bring the free-text export. I want to read all of it, not the summary.
